newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief agrees to Kabila's demand on rights probe.
newsitem.headline: UN chief agrees to Kabila's demand on rights probe.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has agreed to begin an investigation into alleged massacres in the former Zaire during a period beginning March 1, 1993, when refugees began to stream in from Rwanda, according to a letter released on Monday.

Laurent Kabila, whose followers were accused of most of the violations when he was a rebel leader last autumn and before he became president of the new Democratic Republic of the Congo in May, had refused to allow the mission to do its work unless the probe covered periods before his seven-month revolt.

Annan, in a letter to Kabila dated July 15, said that the mandate of the team would now include any violations in the eastern part of the country after March 1, 1993 and that he expected it to report to him no later than December.
He said the names of team members would be released as soon as possible and that "I count on your government to welcome the team, guarantee security and to facilitate their work."

Kabila had turned down an earlier investigation set up by the Geneva-based U.N. Human Rights Commission, objecting to its mandate as well as the team leader, Roberto Garreton of Chile, who has released two critical reports of massacres based on eyewitnesses and other experts.
Consequently, Annan, despite objections from human rights groups, said he was forming his own team without Garreton in order to get the probe underway before evidence disappeared.
Kabila and his forces toppled President Mobutu Sese Seko in May. Kabila has banned political activity and accorded himself, as president, wide-ranging powers.

The original U.N. probe was set up to investigate allegations that Kabila's fighters or their Rwandan and other Tutsi allies killed Rwandan Hutu refugees during their march across Zaire. Kabila dismisses talk of massacres.
The refugees were among the rump of over a million Rwandan Hutus who fled to Zaire fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide by Hutu hardliners of minority Tutsis. Most returned home in December.
Eight African leaders rallied behind Kabila on Sunday, backing his call the U.N. probe be extended beyond the revolt that brought him to power.
